newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish await "Loyalist" reaction to IRA attack.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish await "Loyalist" reaction to IRA attack.

text.p: Pro-British Protestant guerrillas kept Northern Ireland on tenterhooks on Sunday over the fate of their two-year-old truce after fresh hostilities by IRA foes.

The banned Combined Loyalist Military Command, an umbrella group of pro-British Protestant extremists, have held secret meetings to decide whether to retaliate for Irish Republican Army bombs last Monday but have said nothing publicly.
David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of one of the banned groups, said the truce was holding -- for now. But asked about its future, he told Reuters: "No decision has been made."
Ervine, who along with other Loyalist politicians has implored the gunmen not to return to war, cautioned against over-optimism.
"(The situation) is potentially disastrous, yet potentially it could hold," said Ervine whose Progressive Unionist Party is the political arm of the Ulster Volunteer Force.
Fears of Loyalist retaliation mounted after the Catholic-based IRA, in a new blow to faltering peace efforts, switched a bomb campaign from mainland Britain to the province.

IRA fighters breached massive security at British military headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast, last Monday and detonated two 500 lb (225 kg) car bombs, killing a soldier and wounding 30 other people.

Security sources say that abandonment of the ceasefire, which was two years old on Sunday, would herald a resumption of random attacks on the province's Catholic minority and possibly bomb attacks in Dublin and other towns in the Irish Republic.

Dublin's Sunday Tribune newspaper reported that police suspect that a bomb hoax in which a suitcase was left on the steps of Ireland's Central Bank last Thursday was a trial run for a Loyalist attack.

A recognised codeword was used by Loyalists in a warning to the authorities, the paper said. "There is no doubt that Loyalists were delivering a message," an unidentified Irish government source told the newspaper.
Security analysts said a protracted silence by the Loyalist command could be interpreted either as a continuation of the truce or as a warning to the IRA that it could strike back.
To date the CLMC has held dissidents in check but media reports say at least one previously unheard of maverick group has threatened to target republican supporters from midnight on Sunday.
Loyalists extremists fought a 25-year war to buttress British rule and defeat the IRA's aim of an all Ireland state.
Last Monday's IRA bombing was the first in Northern Ireland for two years. The IRA ditched a 17 month ceasefire last February and exploded bombs in British mainland cities.
Loyalist politicians point out they would be expelled from Anglo-Irish sponsored multi-party peace talks, launched in June, if Protestant militants resumed attacks on Catholics.
They say the talks represent the only way forward for the province's Protestant majority and Catholic minority to work out a shared future.
The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, has been excluded from the talks unless its guerrilla allies declare a new ceasefire.
